plan.summary: This tomato has Septoria leaf spot, a fungal disease that spreads by splashing water and survives the winter on debris and tomato-family weeds. Start with clean-up: remove spotted lower leaves, water at the base in the early morning, mulch the soil and pull weeds. Heavy rain and humid days are forecast in early November, so a copper fungicide registered for tomatoes is an optional preventive step before then, used exactly as its label says. Check the plant every few days, clear all plant debris at the end of the season, and plant tomatoes in a different spot next year.

steps.title: Remove spotted lower leaves
steps.detail: Cut off the lower leaves and branches that show small spots with dark edges and pale centres, starting at the bottom of the plant. Do it when the leaves are dry. Bag them and throw them away; don't compost them. Clean your pruners afterwards. Keep doing this whenever new spotted leaves appear.

steps.title: Keep the leaves dry when watering
steps.detail: Water in the early morning, at the soil around the plant rather than over the leaves, for example with drip irrigation or a hose held low. If you must water from above, use low pressure and never do it late in the day. Splashing water carries the spores from leaf to leaf.

steps.title: Mulch the soil around the plant
steps.detail: Spread a layer of organic mulch such as straw, chopped tree leaves or grass clippings over the bare soil around the plant. It stops spores splashing up from the soil onto the lower leaves, which matters before the heavy rain forecast in early November.

steps.title: Pull weeds and volunteer tomatoes
steps.detail: Pull weeds around the tomato, especially tomato-family weeds such as nightshades, and pull up any volunteer tomato plants. Septoria leaf spot can survive the winter on weeds related to tomato.

steps.title: Optional: protect healthy leaves before the rain
steps.detail: Rain and a long humid stretch are forecast from early November, when the disease spreads fastest. If you choose to protect the remaining healthy leaves, apply a copper fungicide registered for use on tomatoes where you live before the rain, and follow its label exactly, including how long to wait between spraying and picking. Fungicides only protect healthy leaves; they don't cure spotted ones and work only together with the clean-up steps above.
steps.safety_note: Use only a product registered for this use where you live, and follow its label exactly.

steps.title: Check for new spots
steps.detail: Check the plant for new spots, especially on leaves higher up and after the rain. Note whether spotted leaves are turning yellow and dropping. If the spots look different from before, or the plant declines fast, take a clear, close photo of the top and underside of an affected leaf or contact your local extension office.

steps.title: Clear the plant and debris at season's end
steps.detail: When the season ends, pull out the whole plant and remove as much fallen leaf and stem debris as you can. Bag it and throw it away rather than composting it, because the fungus survives the winter on old debris. Till or break up any debris you can't remove.

steps.title: Plan to rotate tomatoes to a new spot
steps.detail: Next season, plant tomatoes, potatoes, peppers and eggplant in a different spot, and come back to this spot only once every three years. A crop such as corn is a good choice here in between. Give next year's plants room so they don't touch, and stake them so air moves through.

watch_for: New spots appearing on upper leaves within a week after the early November rain, despite removing spotted leaves.
Spotted leaves yellowing and dropping faster than you can remove them over the next two weeks.

Spots appearing on stems or fruit, or spots that look different from before (for example large rings, greasy patches or mould on the underside), at any time: take a clear photo or contact your local extension office.
Septoria spots returning on next year's tomatoes within the first weeks after planting, which would mean the spot or debris still carries the fungus.

plan.summary: This tomato has Septoria leaf spot, a fungal disease spread by splashing water that starts on the lower leaves. Remove spotted leaves now, keep the foliage dry, mulch the soil and improve airflow. Heavy rain and high humidity are forecast for early November, so check the plant often around then. A copper fungicide is an optional extra before the rain, used only as its label directs. At the end of the season, clear weeds, the old plant and its debris so the disease doesn't carry over to next year.

steps.title: Remove spotted lower leaves
steps.detail: Cut off the lower leaves and branches that show the small round spots with dark edges and pale centres. Bag them and throw them away; don't compost them. Work when the leaves are dry, and clean your pruners afterwards so you don't carry spores to healthy leaves.

steps.title: Keep the leaves dry when watering
steps.detail: Water at the base of the plant, ideally with drip or a soaker hose, in the early morning. Avoid overhead watering. If you must water from above, use low pressure and don't do it late in the day, because splashing water spreads the spores from leaf to leaf.

steps.title: Mulch the soil around the plant
steps.detail: Spread a layer of organic mulch such as straw, chopped leaves or grass clippings over the soil around the plant. It stops spores in the soil splashing up onto the leaves. This matters especially with heavy rain expected in early November.

steps.title: Prune and stake for better airflow
steps.detail: Remove suckers and tie the plant to its stake or trellis so air moves through the foliage and the leaves dry faster after dew or rain. Prune only when the plant is dry.

steps.title: Check for new spots
steps.detail: Check the plant every few days, starting with the lower leaves and working up. Remove newly spotted leaves as you find them. Pay close attention after the wet spell forecast for early November. If you see spots on the fruit or spots that don't look like Septoria, take a clear close-up photo or contact your local extension office.

steps.title: Optional: protect leaves before the wet spell
steps.detail: Fungicides only protect healthy leaves and won't cure spotted ones, so use one alongside the clean-up steps. Before the heavy rain and humid days forecast for early November, you can apply a copper fungicide registered for tomatoes where you live. Follow its label exactly, including the waiting period between spraying and picking, before you harvest any fruit.
steps.safety_note: Use only a product registered for this use where you live, and follow its label exactly.

steps.title: Clear weeds and volunteer tomatoes
steps.detail: Pull weeds in and around the bed, especially tomato-family weeds such as nightshades, and any volunteer tomato plants. Septoria survives the winter on some weeds related to tomato.

steps.title: Clear the plant and debris at season's end
steps.detail: When the plant has finished for the season, pull it out and remove as much fallen leaf and stem debris as you can. Bag it and throw it away. Till in any debris you can't remove so it breaks down quickly, since the fungus survives the winter on old debris. Next year, plant tomatoes and their relatives in a different spot.

watch_for: New spots still appearing on the middle and upper leaves a week after the early November rain, despite removing infected leaves.
Spotted leaves yellowing and dropping faster than new growth replaces them over the next two weeks.
Spots on the fruit or stems, or spots that look different from Septoria, at any time: take a clear close-up photo or contact your local extension office.

plan.summary: This late tomato has Septoria leaf spot, a fungal disease that spreads by splashing water and thrives in humid, wet weather. Start with clean-up and airflow: remove spotted leaves, water at the soil, prune and stake, mulch and clear weeds. Heavy rain and long humid spells are forecast in early November, so finish these steps before then; a preventive copper fungicide is an optional extra, used only as its label directs. At the end of the season, clear away all plant debris so the disease does not carry over.

steps.title: Remove spotted lower leaves
steps.detail: While the plant is dry, cut off the lower leaves and branches that show the small spots with dark edges and pale centres. Bag them and put them in the rubbish, not the compost. Clean your pruners afterwards. Keep doing this whenever new spotted leaves appear.

steps.title: Keep the leaves dry when watering
steps.detail: Water in the early morning at the soil around the plant, for example with a drip line or a watering can held low, not over the leaves. If you must water from above, avoid the late afternoon and evening and use a gentle flow so water does not splash spores from leaf to leaf.

steps.title: Prune and stake for airflow
steps.detail: On a dry day, remove suckers and tie the plant to a stake or trellis so air moves through it and the leaves dry faster after dew or rain. Make sure it does not touch neighbouring plants.

steps.title: Mulch the soil around the plant
steps.detail: Cover the bare soil under the plant with a layer of organic mulch such as straw, chopped tree leaves or grass clippings. It stops spores splashing up from the soil onto the leaves, which matters before the heavy rain forecast in early November.

steps.title: Check for new spots
steps.detail: Check the plant for new spots, especially on leaves higher up than the ones you removed. Note whether spots are spreading upward and remove newly spotted leaves. If spots appear on stems or fruit, or look different, take a clear close-up photo or contact your local extension office.

steps.title: Clear weeds and volunteer tomatoes
steps.detail: Pull weeds in and around the bed, especially tomato relatives such as nightshades and ground cherry, and pull up any volunteer tomato plants. Septoria leaf spot can survive on tomato-related weeds.

steps.title: Consider a preventive fungicide before the rain
steps.detail: Optional, only alongside the steps above. Heavy rain and long humid spells are forecast in early November, when the disease spreads fastest. If you choose to protect the remaining healthy leaves, use a copper fungicide registered for tomatoes where you live and follow its label exactly, including the waiting time between spraying and picking. Fungicides only prevent new infections; they do not cure spotted leaves. Apply on a dry, calm day before the rain.
steps.safety_note: Use only a product registered for this use where you live, and follow its label exactly.

steps.title: Clear the plant and debris at season's end
steps.detail: When the plant finishes for the season, pull it out and remove as much fallen leaf and plant debris as you can. Bag it and throw it away, since the disease survives the winter on old debris. Till in anything left behind. Next season, grow tomatoes and their relatives in a different spot.

watch_for: New spots on upper leaves within a week of removing the spotted lower leaves.
Spots spreading quickly up the plant in the week after the heavy rain forecast for early November.
Many leaves yellowing and dropping over the next two weeks despite the clean-up steps.
Spots or lesions appearing on stems or fruit at any time; if so, send a clear photo or contact your local extension office.
